title: Teaching & Education
tagline: Become a teacher the deliberate way — licensure, classroom craft, assessment, and leadership paths.
summary: Teaching is a licensed profession with a well-defined on-ramp: a bachelor's with educator preparation, state certification exams, and student teaching — followed by a craft that takes years to master. This roadmap covers the licensure path, classroom management and planning skills, assessment, reaching every learner, and the growth routes (National Board, coaching, administration).

sources.label: BLS OOH — Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers

detail.description: Teaching blends subject expertise, performance, counseling, and project management — daily, in front of young people. The joy is real; so is the workload: planning, grading, families, and accountability.
detail.why: Teaching is a licensed, structured profession — going in with eyes open about the reality (not the movie version) is the single best predictor of staying and thriving.
learn: Read the BLS profile of elementary teachers and O*NET task lists
Talk to 3 working teachers: best day, worst day, weekly hours
Tutor one student for a month and reflect weekly
List what attracts you and what worries you — check both against reality

resources.title: BLS OOH — Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers

tasks: Prepare objectives and outlines for courses of study, following curriculum guidelines or requirements of states and schools.

detail.description: Teaching careers span public K-12 (licensed), private and charter schools (rules vary), early childhood, special education, adult education, and non-school settings: museums, corporate training, tutoring, ESL abroad.
detail.why: Licensure requirements differ by setting — knowing which door you want changes your degree and exam choices.
learn: Compare public, private, and charter requirements in your state
Explore special education as a distinct (high-demand) path
List non-school teaching settings that don't require state licensure
Pick a primary target and a backup setting

resources.title: BLS OOH — Education, Training, and Library occupations

detail.description: Your certification will name a grade band (early childhood, elementary, middle, high school) and subject or subjects. Elementary certifications are broad; secondary certifications are content-deep.
detail.why: This choice shapes your exams, coursework, and daily reality. High-need subjects (special education, math, science, bilingual) often carry incentives.
learn: List grade bands with their daily realities (self-contained vs rotating periods)
Check your state's certification areas and which are designated shortage areas
Assess your content strength honestly (can you explain it five ways?)
Note shortage-area incentives: stipends, loan forgiveness

resources.title: U.S. Department of Education — teacher shortage areas

detail.description: Sitting in real classrooms — as a volunteer, paraprofessional, or observer — shows you pacing, management, and the invisible work teachers do before and after students arrive.
detail.why: Hours of observation are often required for program admission anyway, and they convert your decision from guess to evidence.
learn: Arrange observations across two grade bands if possible
Log what the teacher does besides teaching (timing, transitions, data)
Note 3 management moves you'd steal and why
Reflect: energy level after a full day in a classroom

resources.title: Edutopia — classroom practice videos and articles

detail.description: The standard route is a bachelor's degree that includes an approved educator preparation program — coursework in pedagogy plus supervised clinical practice. Program quality and placement support vary widely.
detail.why: Your prep program's reputation and clinical placements affect both your licensure and your first job offers.
learn: Verify state approval/accreditation for any program you consider
Compare traditional university vs preparation-program-only routes
Map prerequisites you can complete at community-college cost
Ask programs: placement rate, mentor support, first-year alumni outcomes

detail.description: Most states require standardized licensure exams — commonly ETS Praxis tests covering core academic skills, pedagogy, and subject-specific content; some states use their own tests instead.
detail.why: Exams are gatekeeping events with real scheduling and fees. Knowing exactly which ones your state requires prevents semester-losing surprises.
learn: List your state's exact required exams for your certification area
Take a full-length practice test and score it honestly
Build a 6–8 week study plan around weak domains
Register early — test seats and score reporting take weeks

detail.description: Student teaching is a full-time supervised placement — typically a semester — where you gradually take over planning, instruction, assessment, and management under a mentor teacher and university supervisor.
detail.why: It is the true apprenticeship of teaching. What you put in (initiative, reflection, relationships) determines your readiness and your references.
learn: Co-plan with your mentor from week one
Teach full days progressively; video yourself and review
Keep a daily reflection journal (what worked, what to change)
Build a portfolio artifact set: plans, assessments, student work

detail.description: State education agencies issue teaching licenses: application, exams, program verification, background clearance, and fees. Initial licenses often carry induction requirements and renewal cycles.
detail.why: The license is the profession's gateway — and it's state-specific, which matters if you might move.
learn: Read your state's licensure page end-to-end (requirements, fees, timelines)
Understand initial vs professional/standard license tiers
Learn license reciprocity basics before planning interstate moves
Calendar renewal and PD requirements from day one

certs.name: State Teaching License
certs.note: Issued after an approved preparation program, required exams, and background clearance; requirements and titles vary by state.

resources.title: U.S. Department of Education — state contacts

detail.description: Alternative certification lets degree-holders teach while completing pedagogy requirements — often while employed as the teacher of record, with heavy first-year support.
detail.why: It is the most common route for career changers, and high-need subjects frequently offer it with stipends.
learn: Find your state's approved alternative routes
Compare cost and support vs a full preparation program
Understand provisional/intern license conditions
Interview one alternatively certified teacher about their first year

detail.description: A master's can serve three purposes: initial licensure (M.A.T. programs for degree-holders), salary advancement (many districts pay more for graduate credits), or specialization (special education, TESOL, reading, leadership).
detail.why: Timing matters: a M.A.T. makes sense before licensure; salary-lane credits often make sense after — doing it in the wrong order wastes money.
learn: Check your district's salary schedule for graduate-credit lanes
Compare M.A.T. (licensure) vs M.Ed. (advanced) purposes
Calculate payback period for tuition against the salary bump
Consider endorsements (ESOL, special ed, reading) as cheaper specializations

resources.title: BLS OOH — Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers

detail.description: Effective lessons start from the end: what students should know and do (objective), how you'll know they got there (assessment), then the activities — the backward design logic (Wiggins & McTighe).
detail.why: Planning is where teaching is actually won. Clear objectives and aligned checks turn chaotic days into purposeful ones.
learn: Write objectives students can understand ('I can…' statements)
Design a lesson backward: objective → assessment → activity
Plan the opening 5 minutes and closing 5 minutes deliberately
Build one full lesson and teach it; revise from evidence

detail.description: Public teaching aligns to standards — state standards for each grade and subject (e.g., state adoptions of Common Core-style standards), delivered through adopted curriculum and pacing guides.
detail.why: Standards define what you're accountable for; curriculum defines the 'how'. Reading both fluently is a day-one professional skill.
learn: Locate your state's standards for one grade/subject
Unpack one standard into teachable learning targets
Map a week of an adopted curriculum against the standards
Identify gaps you'd supplement and how

detail.description: Classroom management is the system that makes learning possible: clear expectations, predictable routines, relationships, calm consistency, and low-key correction before escalation.
detail.why: New teachers overwhelmingly cite management as their hardest challenge. Proactive systems beat reactive discipline in every study of practice.
learn: Draft your top 5 non-negotiable expectations and how you'll teach them
Script your first two weeks of routines explicitly
Practice the least-invasive correction ladder (proximity, eye contact, quiet word)
Observe a veteran teacher and count their management moves in 30 minutes

detail.description: Questions drive thinking: open vs closed, wait time, cold-calling with warmth, follow-up probes ('say more', 'why?'), and checks for understanding after every segment.
detail.why: Questioning is the steering wheel of a lesson — it turns a lecture into thinking and reveals misconceptions in real time.
learn: Practice 3-second wait time (it feels long; it works)
Write a question ladder: recall → explain → apply → justify
Try cold-call with names prepared in advance
Add a check-for-understanding to every 10-minute segment

detail.description: Engagement is attention plus effort: relevance, choice, collaboration, movement, and appropriately challenging tasks. It is designed, not hoped for.
detail.why: Behavior problems are often engagement problems. Teachers who can design absorbing work spend far less energy on discipline.
learn: Audit a lesson: what % of students were actively thinking at minute 20?
Add one element of student choice to a planned lesson
Use think-pair-share and count participation breadth
Design a task students would do even without a grade

detail.description: Practical classroom tech: learning management systems (Google Classroom, Canvas), presentation tools, formative-assessment apps, and accessibility features — chosen for learning value, not novelty.
detail.why: Districts assume LMS fluency; smart tech use also saves hours of grading and communication time.
learn: Set up a course in a free LMS (Google Classroom or Canvas free tier)
Use one digital check-for-understanding tool in a mock lesson
Learn your platform's parent/family communication features
Set boundaries: tech should serve the objective, not drive it

detail.description: Assessment spans formative (checking during learning) and summative (measuring at milestones), with rubrics, clear criteria, and grading policies that measure learning rather than compliance.
detail.why: Grades communicate — to students, families, and next-year teachers. Fair, transparent assessment is both an equity issue and a skill.
learn: Write a 4-level rubric for one authentic task
Design 3 formative checks for a single lesson
Compare zero-heavy vs evidence-based grading policies
Regrade one sample with your rubric and check consistency

detail.description: Using assessment data to reteach, regroup, and plan: item analysis, error patterns, small-group formation, and progress monitoring over weeks.
detail.why: Modern schools run on data cycles. Teachers who move from 'gave the test' to 'changed Tuesday because of the test' stand out immediately.
learn: Analyze a class assessment by item and error type
Form 3 flexible small groups from the results
Plan a reteach for the two weakest standards
Track one metric (e.g., mastery %) over 4 weeks

detail.description: Differentiation adjusts content, process, or product to learner readiness, interest, or profile — tiered tasks, choice boards, flexible grouping — without writing 30 separate lesson plans.
detail.why: Every class spans years of reading levels. Sustainable differentiation (structures, not per-child plans) is the professional middle path.
learn: Build a tiered task set (below/on/above) for one objective
Try a choice board with 6 options and one required element
Use flexible groups that change by skill, never by 'ability label'
Differentiate one homework task in two minutes flat

detail.description: Universal Design for Learning plans for variability from the start: multiple means of representation, action/expression, and engagement (CAST framework) — benefiting everyone, required for some.
detail.why: UDL reduces the need for retrofitted accommodations and is increasingly embedded in teacher evaluation and law.
learn: Read the three UDL principles at udlguidelines.cast.org
Redesign one lesson with two means of representation and expression
Check your materials for accessibility basics (captions, readable fonts)
Identify one barrier in your planned lesson and remove it

detail.description: Students with disabilities learn under legal plans: IEPs (Individualized Education Programs, under IDEA) and 504 plans. General-education teachers implement accommodations and attend meetings.
detail.why: You will have students with plans in every class. Implementing accommodations faithfully is both a legal duty and good teaching.
learn: Learn what IDEA guarantees (FAPE, least restrictive environment)
Read a sample IEP: present levels, goals, accommodations
Build an accommodation checklist for your class rosters
Know your role in IEP meetings and documentation

resources.title: IRIS Center — disability resources and modules

detail.description: English language learners need language support inside content teaching: visuals, sentence frames, pre-taught vocabulary, and assessments that separate language from content mastery.
detail.why: ELL populations are growing in nearly every district, and supporting them well is both a legal obligation and a marked teaching skill.
learn: Learn WIDA-style proficiency levels at a high level
Add sentence frames and visuals to one lesson
Pre-teach 5 academic vocabulary words with visuals
Separate language objectives from content objectives in your plan

detail.description: Growth accelerates with structure: induction mentors for new teachers, professional learning communities (PLCs) that analyze data and plan together, and peer observation cycles.
detail.why: Isolated teachers plateau; networked teachers compound. Seeking and using mentorship is the highest-ROI professional habit.
learn: Join or form a PLC around one shared course
Run a peer observation exchange twice per semester
Bring one student-work artifact to each PLC meeting
Ask for a mentor explicitly if your school doesn't assign one

detail.description: National Board Certification (NBPTS) is the profession's advanced voluntary credential: a portfolio of practice plus content-knowledge assessment, organized around the Five Core Propositions.
detail.why: Many states reward it with salary stipends or license upgrades, and the process itself is widely described as the best professional development in teaching.
learn: Review the certificate areas and component structure at nbpts.org
Check your state's incentive policy for NBCTs
Talk to an NBCT about the time commitment (roughly 1–3 years)
Decide timing: usually after 3+ years of practice

certs.name: National Board Certification
certs.issuer: National Board for Professional Teaching Standards (NBPTS)
certs.note: Portfolio submission plus assessment center exams; designed for experienced teachers.

detail.description: Deliberate improvement comes from structured reflection: video review, student feedback, journals, and hypothesis-driven tweaks — treating your own classroom as a research site.
detail.why: Experience alone doesn't create expertise; reflected-on experience does. This habit underlies every other growth step on this map.
learn: Video one lesson per month and code your talk ratio and wait time
Collect anonymous student feedback twice a year
Keep a running 'what I changed and why' log
Pick one skill per quarter to improve deliberately

detail.description: Classroom teaching branches into three broad directions: master-teacher track (National Board, mentor, model classrooms), instructional leadership (coach, specialist, department head), and administration (assistant principal → principal → district roles).
detail.why: The profession rewards depth as well as management; knowing the branches early helps you build the right evidence for each.
learn: Map your district's actual roles: coach, TOSA, AP, principal
Compare salary curves across the three branches
Identify which branch matches your energy: students, teachers, or systems
Set a 5-year target and the evidence it requires

resources.title: BLS OOH — Kindergarten and Elementary School Teachers

detail.description: Coaches support teachers one-on-one: co-planning, modeling lessons, observing with non-evaluative feedback, and facilitating data conversations — a teacher-leader role in most districts.
detail.why: Coaching is the most common first step out of the classroom that keeps you close to instruction, often with stipend or schedule advantages.
learn: Learn a coaching model (e.g., student-centered or instructional coaching cycles)
Practice non-evaluative feedback language
Co-plan with a peer for a semester before seeking the role
Note what coaching requires: credibility, discretion, patience

detail.description: Specialists design and support curriculum and intervention at school or district level: reading specialists, math interventionists, TESOL coordinators, and instructional materials leads — usually endorsement-backed.
detail.why: Specialist roles combine expertise with system impact, and endorsements (reading, ESOL, special education) make you both promotable and more effective now.
learn: Identify the endorsement your target specialist role requires
Explore reading-specialist and TESOL endorsement programs
Pilot an intervention group at your school and document results
Present results to your admin — visibility creates the next role

detail.description: School leadership (assistant principal → principal) requires an administrative license (typically a master's in educational leadership plus exam), and the job is part instruction-leader, part operations, part community politics.
detail.why: Principals shape entire school cultures — and administration is where education's largest salaries and widest impact sit.
learn: Review your state's administrator licensure requirements
Shadow an AP or principal for a day
Lead one non-classroom initiative (schedule, event, PD session)
Consider leadership programs that pair licensure with residency

resources.title: O*NET — Education Administrators, Elementary and Secondary School
BLS OOH — Elementary, Middle, and High School Principals

detail.description: Teaching abroad spans licensed international schools (which prefer state certification and experience) and ESL/EFL teaching (where TEFL/TESOL certificates are the standard entry credential).
detail.why: International routes satisfy travel goals and often pay comparably with lower living costs — but licensure vs TEFL determines which tier you enter.
learn: Compare international schools vs language academies honestly
Review TEFL/TESOL certificate basics (120-hour courses are the norm)
Note other countries' licensure equivalents (e.g., UK QTS/PGCE)
Attend an international-recruiting fair if you're licensed

certs.name: TEFL/TESOL Certificate
certs.note: A course-based teaching credential (not state licensure); ~120 hours is the widely accepted standard for EFL teaching roles.

resources.title: BLS OOH — Education, Training, and Library occupations

detail.description: Adjacent education work — private tutoring, test prep, teaching assistants, museum education, corporate training, and curriculum writing — offers flexible entry points and income bridges.
detail.why: These roles let you build teaching evidence before licensure, earn while studying, or shift later without leaving education entirely.
learn: Note the TA path: paraprofessional roles (O*NET 25-9045) often require less schooling
Try 10 hours of paid tutoring to test your fit and pricing
Explore curriculum-writing side work with reputable publishers
Keep evidence of student outcomes for future applications
